section.title: Limits from motion and approximation
section.p: A speedometer gives an instantaneous reading. But if all we have is a position formula, we first see only average velocities over intervals. The limit is the act of shrinking the interval until the average rate settles toward one number.

subsection.title: Average velocity as the interval shrinks
subsection.p: Let s(t)=t^2 be the position of an object moving along a line, measured in meters after t seconds. We want the velocity at the instant t=2.
Over the interval from 2 to 2+h, the average velocity is

Since h\neq 0, we may divide by h: A(h)=4+h.
So the average velocity depends on the width h of the interval:

table.title: Average velocity as interval width shrinks

subsection.p: The closer h is to 0, the closer A(h) is to 4. This suggests that the instantaneous velocity at t=2 should be 4\text{ meters/second}.

statement.p: Instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocities over shrinking intervals:

figure.caption: The slopes of the secant lines approach the slope of the tangent line at t=2.

subsection.p: The same calculation can be read geometrically. The average velocity over an interval is the slope of a secant line. As the second point moves toward t=2, the secant line approaches a tangent line.
This is why limits are needed before derivatives can be defined. A tangent slope is not usually found from two separated points. It is found by letting one point approach another.

subsection.title: Decimal approximations to a number
subsection.p: Limits do not belong only to motion. They also appear whenever approximations close in on a target.
Chapter 2 used nested intervals to trap \sqrt{2}:

The left endpoints 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, 1.4142, \dots approach \sqrt{2} from below. The right endpoints approach it from above. Neither finite list equals the whole number \sqrt{2}, but the approximations can be made as close as desired.

A simpler example is 1.9, 1.99, 1.999, 1.9999, \dots. These numbers approach 2. The error after n decimal places is a power of 10: 2-1.9=0.1, 2-1.99=0.01, 2-1.999=0.001. The errors approach 0, so the approximations approach 2.

principle.title: A limit is a target value for a process

statement.p: A number can be approached by decimal approximations. A velocity can be approached by average velocities. A tangent slope can be approached by secant slopes.

subsection.p: The same idea appears in different clothing. The mathematics is the same: errors are forced to become small.

subsection.title: The informal meaning of a limit
subsection.p: Let f be a function. When we write
we mean: as x gets close to a, the values f(x) get close to L.
The notation is read: the limit of f(x) as x approaches a is L.
There is one detail that must be said early: x\to a does not mean x=a. It means x is close to a. In many limits, the value at x=a is not used at all.

statement.p: We write \lim_{x\to a} f(x)=L if the values f(x) can be made as close to L as desired by taking x sufficiently close to a, with x\neq a.
If x is close to 3, then 2x+5 is close to 2(3)+5=11. So
Here nothing strange happens at x=3. We can find the limit by direct substitution.

example.title: The value at the point may not matter

statement.p: Near x=1, but not at x=1, the function behaves like 2x+1. As x\to 1, 2x+1\to 3. Therefore

figure.caption: The limit watches nearby values. It does not have to equal the value of the function at the point.

warning.title: Limit versus value at a point
warning.p: A limit near a is not the same thing as the value at a.
When the two do agree, we will have a special property called continuity.

subsection.title: Limits from graphs and tables
subsection.p: A graph can suggest a limit. A table can suggest a limit. But both must be read with care.

example.title: A table that suggests a limit

statement.p: Let g(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x-1} for x\neq 1. The formula is not defined at x=1, but we can still examine values near 1:
The values approach 2. So the table suggests \lim_{x\to 1}\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}=2.

example.title: A graph that suggests no limit

statement.p: Define J(x)=\frac{|x|}{x} for x\neq 0. If x\gt 0, J(x)=1. If x\lt 0, J(x)=-1.
The values near 0 do not approach one common number. From the right they stay at 1; from the left they stay at -1. Therefore

figure.caption: A two-sided limit exists only when nearby values approach one common target.

principle.title: A limit must have one target

statement.p: A two-sided limit exists only when nearby values from both sides approach one single, common target value.

subsection.title: What a limit can ignore
subsection.p: The limit \lim_{x\to a}f(x) ignores the value f(a). It watches what happens near a.

table.title: Three possible relationships between f(a) and \lim_{x\to a}f(x)

row.cell: f(a) exists and equals the limit
f(a) exists but differs from the limit
f(a) does not exist, but the limit exists

subsection.p: The first situation is the calm one. The second and third are warning signs. They show why limits must come before continuity.
The next task is practical. Graphs and tables help us guess limits, but calculus needs reliable ways to calculate them. Algebra gives the first tools.
